newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi court to get proof from heirs in nurses case.
newsitem.headline: Saudi court to get proof from heirs in nurses case.

text.p: Lawyers will on Monday offer proof the mother and brother of an Australian nurse killed in Saudi Arabia are her heirs and could demand execution if the alleged killers are found guilty, sources close to the case said.

An Islamic sharia court called for the proof last week at the fourth session in the trial of two British nurses accused of the crime. Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, are charged with murdering their colleague Yvonne Gilford in December at a medical complex in the eastern city of Dhahran.
"They (the court) already have documentation to that effect and they wanted additional documentation," a source close to the proceedings told Reuters on Sunday. "This will be forthcoming."
The court adjourned on June 15 and the trial resumes on Monday. The Gilfords have not come to Saudi Arabia and are represented in court by the Saudi-based International Law Firm.
Yvonne Gilford was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the King Fahd military medical complex, just days before her 56th birthday.
If the two women are found guilty of murdering Gilford, they may face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally public beheading by the sword.
The two have said they were forced into making confessions, which they later revoked. Both women say they are innocent.

Legal sources said the question of rightful heirs was one of two critical issues currently at stake. The legal heirs would by Islamic sharia law enforced in the kingdom have the right to decide for or against execution if the court finds the accused guilty and says capital punishment is the appropriate sentence.

Gilford's brother Frank, who has so far spoken out as the legal heir, has said he favours the death penalty. The victim's 84-year-old mother Muriel suffers from Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home in Australia.

The other issue is Frank's power of attorney, the sources said. The court has refused to accept the power of attorney from the victim's mother to her son "until it is established that the power of attorney was given when Mrs M. L. Gilford was mentally competent", the defence lawyer Salah al-Hejailan has said.
The sources close to the case said proof clarifying the power of attorney would also be provided on Monday by the lawyers representing the victim's family.

Legal experts said the court was being very careful to ensure procedural due process. "They want whatever result they come to to be reliable on the merits and sustainable on the procedures," one said.
The case of the two British nurses has stirred up controversy since they were arrested in December, sparking calls for a more open, public trial.
Saudi officials, who have barred journalists from the trial, have repeatedly said the proceedings were fair and that the women had nothing to fear if they are innocent.
Witnesses said although the trial was in Arabic, the defendants had access to translators.

"There are two translators," one said. "All of the Arabic-speaking lawyers who are attending the trial on the defence team speak English and so they offer translation and advice to the nurses and inform them about what's going on."
Parry and McLauchlan have attended all hearings so far, coming from their cells at the nearby Dammam central prison.
